entries.meaning: God is my strong man
Worker of the earth
Worker of the earth
entries.note: The feminine form of George. The country Georgia has an unrelated origin.

entries.meaning: God is gracious
entries.note: A short form of Giovanna and a variant of Ioanna, both related to John.
entries.origin: Italian and Greek, with Hebrew roots

entries.meaning: Grace
entries.note: An English virtue name.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Gabriel.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Gabriel.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Gabriella and Gabrielle.

entries.meaning: See Gabriel.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Gabriel.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Gabriele.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian, equivalent to English Gabriel.

entries.meaning: From Italian Gabriella. By surface analysis, Gabriel + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian [in turn from Hebrew], masculine equivalent Gabriel.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Gabrielle, feminine form of Gabriel (see there for more).
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Short form of Gabrielle.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew גָּד (gad), a son of Jacob.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From French Gaëtan and Gaétan, from Italian Gaetano, from Latin Caiētānus.
entries.note: A male given name from French, equivalent to English Cajetan.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गगन (gagana).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: An occupational surname from Middle English gage, guage (“measure”) for an assayer, or gage (“pledge”) for a moneylender.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of modern usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Γαῖᾰ (Gaîă, “Gaea, the Earth personified as a goddess”), from γαῖᾰ (gaîă, “the Earth”), probably related to γῆ (gê, “earth, land; country”).
entries.note: A female given name inspired by Mother Earth.

entries.meaning: From Latin Gaisericus, from Vandalic *Gaisarīx, itself from Proto-Germanic *Gaizarīks. Doublet of Garrick.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, of historical usage, notably borne by a Vandalic King who ruled over North Africa.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Gaius
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, of rare usage

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गजानन (gajānana)
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit commonly used in India.

entries.meaning: From Old French Galahad, of obscure origin and meaning. Suggestions include Old Welsh, or biblical Gilead.
entries.note: A male given name from the Celtic languages in occasional use since the 19th century.
entries.origin: the Celtic languages in occasional use since the 19th century

entries.meaning: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of mostly American usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Bulgarian and Russian Гали́на (Galína), from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Bulgarian or Russian female given name Гали́на (Galína).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ukrainian Гали́на (Halýna), from Ancient Greek γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm”), name of a Nereid and of early martyrs venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Ukrainian female given name Гали́на (Halýna).

entries.meaning: From Middle English Gamaliel, from Late Latin Gamaliēl, from Koine Greek Γαμαλιήλ (Gamaliḗl), from Aramaic גַמַלִיאיֵל (Ḡamalīʾēl), from Biblical Hebrew גַּמְלִיאֵל (Gamlīʾēl). Compare Classical Syriac ܓ݂ܰܡܰܠܺܝܐܝܶܠ (Ḡamalīʾēl).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew (“God is my reward”).

entries.meaning: The source of the legend of Gambrinus is uncertain and perhaps based on a mythical Germanic king Gambrivius. The etymology is unknown, but many explanations exist: * a corruption of Jean Primus, John I, Duke of Brabant (1252–1294) * Middle High German gambra (“germination of grain”) * cambier, name given to brewers in the north of France in the Middle Ages
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From Old Norse mythology Gandalfr (“elf familiar”). It may be reinforced by various similar names in Medieval Latin, like a few saints and clergymen.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages known in history, and in the books of Tolkien, but not usually bestowed on children.
entries.origin: the Germanic languages known in history

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Gandolf.
entries.note: A male given name from German.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गणेश (gaṇeśa).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Hindi गंगा (gaṅgā) or Sanskrit गङ्गा (gaṅgā). Doublet of Ganges.
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit गङ्गाधर (gaṅgādhara, “‘Ganges-receiver’, the ocean; ‘Ganges-supporter’, Name of Siva.”); ultimately from गङ्गा (gaṅgā, “the river Ganges”) + धर (dhara).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: Derived from Irish Mag Fhionnáin "son of Finan".
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Of Old Welsh origin and cognate with the Welsh name Geraint (from Latin Gerontius (“old man”), from Ancient Greek γέρων (gérōn, “old man”)) or perhaps the word gwareddawg, gwaredd (“gentleness”); see gwâr (“gentle”).
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh of Welsh origin; name of a knight in the Arthurian romance.

entries.meaning: Also Garfeld, from Old English gār (“spear”) + feld (“field”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गरिमा (garimā, “dignity, prestige”).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: English surname, from the noun garland. Also derived from Garland in Devon, from an ancestor of the noun gore (“triangular piece of land”) + land.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Named after the garnet gemstone.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Variant of Garrett.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: A medieval English and Irish form of the Germanic given names Gerard and Gerald. Of Old High German origin.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, transferred from an English and an Irish surname, or in Ireland directly from Gerard.

entries.meaning: From Old English *Gārrīċ (from gār (“spear”) + rīċ), from Proto-Germanic *Gaizarīks. Doublet of Gaiseric.
entries.note: A male given name from Old English.

entries.meaning: Welsh garth probably has its influence on Welsh place names.
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh, shortened form of Gareth

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गर्वित (garvita, “proud”).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गर्विता (garvitā, “proud”).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Medieval short form of Germanic compound names beginning with gari or geri ("spear"), such as Gerard, Garrett, Gerald, or Gerbert. Cognate with the Scottish and Irish name Garaidh. Sometimes also a short form of Gareth. The popularity of the given name in the 20th century is due to the American actor Gary Cooper, whose stage name was invented by his agent, a native of Gary, Indiana.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, popular from the 1940s to the 1970s; variant form Garry.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गौरांग (gaurāṃga).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गौरव (gaurava).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गौरी (gaurī).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Sanskrit गौतम (gautama)
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गौतम (gautama).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India; more often romanised as Gautam.

entries.meaning: Medieval variant of Gawain, the name of an Arthurian knight, first recorded as Old French Gauvain. The form Gavin survived in Scotland and spread to other English-speaking countries in the 1960s. Doublet of Gawain.
entries.note: A male given name from the Celtic languages.

entries.meaning: From Russian Гаврии́л (Gavriíl). Doublet of Gabriel.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Russian male given name Гаврии́л (Gavriíl).

entries.meaning: Rare spelling variant of Gavin.
entries.note: A male given name from the Celtic languages.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गायत्री (gāyatrī).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: gay (“homosexual”) + Abraham
entries.note: A respelling of the given name Abraham, insinuating homosexuality.

entries.meaning: Spelling variant of Gay.
entries.note: A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: Derived from the Old French surname Gaillard (from gaillard (“strong”)), via Anglo-Norman. Compare Spanish Gallardo (from gallardo (“dashing, strapping, gallant”). Shaped by folk etymology into gay + lord.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, popular in the 20th century until the 1960s.

entries.meaning: From Gareth (or any personal name starting Ga-) + -zza.
entries.note: A nickname for the given name Gareth or Gary.

entries.meaning: Northern English surname of debated meaning.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीत (gīta).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीतांजलि (gītāṃjali).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीतिका (gītikā).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Malayalam ഗീവർഗീസ് (gīvaṟgīsŭ), probably from Classical Syriac ܓܝܘܪܓܝܣ (gēwargis).
entries.note: A male given name from Malayalam, equivalent to English George.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Middle English Geffrey.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, a medieval spelling of Geoffrey, rarely used today.

entries.meaning: From Latin Geisericus, from a later form of the Vandalic *Gaisarīx, itself from Proto-Germanic *Gaizarīks.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin. Mainly Historical. Name of a Vandalic King who ruled over North Africa.

entries.meaning: From Latin Gelāsius.
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage, notably borne by Pope Gelasius I and Pope Gelasius II.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Latin gemma (“jewel”). The given name is mostly borrowed via Italian Gemma; the spelling Jemma in particular is associated with James. Doublet of gemma and gem.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “creation, beginning, origin”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek of American usage since the 1980s.
entries.origin: Ancient Greek of American usage since the 1980s

entries.meaning: Mentioned in Latin texts as Genava. Probably via a Proto-Celtic *genwā from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénw-eh₂ (“knee”), a derivative of *ǵónu in the sense of a bending river or estuary, possibly akin to Genoa.
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the place name or confused with Genevieve or Ginevra.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Geneviève (patron saint of Paris), from Latin Genovefa, Genoveva, possibly either of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”), or of Celtic origin, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *genos (“family, clan”).
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: A variant of Jenna with the spelling possibly influenced by Gina or Gianna.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Russian Генна́дий (Gennádij).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Russian male given name Генна́дий (Gennádij).

entries.meaning: From Latin Gensericus.
entries.note: A male given name of mainly historical use, borne by a king of the Vandals.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Geoffrey.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Geoffrey.

entries.meaning: From Geoff + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Geoffrey.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Geffrey, from an Old French aristocratic name, Geoffroi [dʒɔfreʲ] (> West Middle French Geoffrey, East Middle French Geoffroy), itself from Proto-French forms (latinized in -us) Jotfredus, Jozsfredus, Josfredus (10th century) and Jof[f]redus, Jofridus, Jaufredus, Geffredus (11th century), and ultimately of Proto-Germanic origin. The second element is *friþuz (“peace, sanctuary”).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, popular in the U.K. in the 20th century.

entries.meaning: Diminutive of George + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name George.

entries.meaning: From Danish, Estonian, Faroese, German, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish Georg, from Latin Geōrgius. The slang sense is from Spiders Georg.
entries.note: A male given name, a Scandinavian and continental Germanic variant of George.

entries.meaning: From Georgia + Ann.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Georges.
entries.note: A male given name from French, equivalent to English George.

entries.meaning: From George + -etta. Piecewise doublet of Georgette.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From French Georgette. By surface analysis, George + -ette. Piecewise doublet of Georgetta.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Diminutives + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name George.

entries.meaning: From French Géorgienne.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: From George + -ina, feminine form of George. Piecewise doublet of Georgine.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From French Georgine. By surface analysis, George + -ine. Piecewise doublet of Georgina.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Greek Γεώργιος (Geórgios), a male given name used in (modern) Greece. Cognate with English George.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Greek male given name Γεώργιος (Geórgios).

entries.meaning: From George + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name George.

entries.meaning: From Welsh Geraint, from Latin Gerontius, Latinized Greek for "old man," from Ancient Greek γέρων (gérōn, “old man”).
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: From Old French, ultimately from Frankish *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *wald (“might, power”). The name was brought to England by the Normans. It survived in Ireland, and was revived in the 19th century.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Gerald + -ine. c. 1540 by the Earl of Surrey as a poetic name for Lady Elizabeth Fitzgerald, "one of the Fitzgeralds". Taken up as a given name in the 19th century, and used as a feminine form of Gerald.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Γεράσιμος (Gerásimos).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Belarusian male given name Гера́сім (Hjerásim)

entries.meaning: Latinate variant of Scandinavian Gerd, from Old Norse Gerðr, garðr (“protection”). The name occurs in nineteenth century Swedish poetry and in Hans Christian Andersen's Snow Queen (1844).
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages occasionally used in English, mostly around 1900.
entries.origin: the Germanic languages occasionally used in English

entries.meaning: Shortening; compare Jerry from Gerald.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Geraldine, also used as a formal given name.

entries.meaning: A patronymic from a medieval given name, identical with the French one; or from an ethnic term for a German.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish). Not related to german (“closely related”) or germane (from the Latin adjective germānus, through Old French). Attested since at least 1520. Replaced the older terms Almain and Dutch (from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz) in English.
entries.note: A male given name from Russian.

entries.meaning: A less common spelling of Gerard.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Clipping + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given names Gerald and Gerard.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew גֵּרְשֹׁם (gershóm, “Gershom”), found in Exodus.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Diminutive + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Gertrude.

entries.meaning: From Old French [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *gaizaz (“spear”) + *þrūþiz (“strength”) or *trut- (“maiden, dear”) ; name of a Belgian seventh century saint.
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Name of an early saint, Latin Gervasius, of unknown meaning, possibly Latinized from some Germanic name: Proto-Germanic *gaizaz (“spear”), second element of uncertain meaning, possibly vallis (“valley”), Proto-Celtic *wastos (“servant”), or the Brythonic name for the river Isara.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, common in the Middle Ages but rare today.

entries.meaning: Said to be named after a nearby lake of the same name.
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: * (name from Italian): Borrowed from Italian Gia * (name from Greek): Clipping of Georgia.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Italian Giancarlo.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: From Italian Gianluca (literally “John-Luke”).
entries.note: A male given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Greek Γιάννης (Giánnis), a male given name used in (modern) Greece. Doublet of John.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Greek male given name Γιάννης (Giánnis).

entries.meaning: Derived from a Middle English diminutive of the name Gilbert
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Gibb + -son.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hebrew גִּדְעוֹן (gid'ón, “Gideon”) ("feller", "hewer", "mighty warrior").
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew, popularized by Puritans.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Gigi. Sometimes a pet form of English names such as Virginia or Genesis. Occasionally from initials G.G. (e.g. George General 'Gigi' Gryce).
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sinhalese ගිහාන් (Gihān).
entries.note: A male given name from Sinhalese, of Sri Lankan origin.

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Gilbert.

entries.meaning: From Old French Gislebert, from Proto-Germanic *Gīslaberhtaz, from *gīslaz (“pledge”) + *berhtaz (“bright, famous”).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew גִּלְעָד (gilʻád). For sense 3, the fictional Gilead theocracy from "The Handmaid's Tale" named itself as such because it presented its oppressive policies as "healing" for a fertility crisis.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew in occasional use.

entries.meaning: Medieval English form of Old French saints' name Giles, modern Gilles, an altered form of Latin Aegīdius, from Ancient Greek Αἰγίδιος (Aigídios), derivative of αἰγίδιον (aigídion, “kid, young goat”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname, converged from variants of Giles (sometimes through Dutch), Julian, and William. * As a northern English surname, from Middle English gil (“ravine, glen”), from Old Norse gil. The Old Norse is also a source of the Norwegian surname. * As an Irish and Scottish Gaelic surname, variant of McGill. * Also as an Irish surname, variant of Gall.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given names Giles, Julian, and William, of medieval usage.

entries.meaning: From a Middle English diminutive of the male given name Giles.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic gille (“servant lad”) + Moire (“Mary mother of Jesus”).
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: A name from Old Norse.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: * (name from Greek): Clipping of Georgina. * (name from Latin): Clipping of Regina. * (name from Italian): Italian Gina
entries.note: A female given name. Diminutive of names ending in -gina A diminutive of the female given name Georgina, from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Italian Ginevra. Doublet of Jennifer.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian, variant of Guinevere.

entries.meaning: Clipped form of Ginger, itself sometimes a nickname for Virginia.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Ginger and Virginia.

entries.meaning: A diminutive of Virginia; also a nickname for someone or something with ginger-coloured hair.
entries.note: A female given name from English and nickname. Popularized by actress Ginger Rogers

entries.meaning: From French Ginnette, a diminutive of Geneviève with -ette.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Diminutive + -ie
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Virginia and Ginevra.

entries.meaning: Diminutive + -y
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Virginia and Ginevra.

entries.meaning: From Italian Gio.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given names Giovanni, Giovani, Giorgi, Giorgio, Giuseppe, and Sergio, from Italian.

entries.meaning: From Italian Giovanni (“John”).
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Giovanni. Doublet of John.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गिरिजा (girijā).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Giselle.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीता (gītā, “song”), sometimes in reference to Bhagavad Gita.
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit, used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीतांजलि (gītāṃjali).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गीतिका (gītikā).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Danish Gitte.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Birgitte, from Danish.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Giuseppe.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian, equivalent to English Joseph.

entries.meaning: From gladiol(us) + -a.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Anglicized from Welsh Gwladus, of uncertain origin, perhaps connected with gwlad (“country”).
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: Coined in the twentieth century from Welsh glân (“holy, fair”) and da (“good”).
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: From male given name Glen, from Scottish glen (“secluded valley”).
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, in quiet use since the 19th century.

entries.meaning: A twentieth century coinage from Welsh glân (“clean, holy”) + -ys.
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: Possibly from glory or Glor(ia) + -ania. Compare rare Glora and Gloriana.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Latin gloria (“glory”), first used as a name in 19th-century literature.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, popular during the first half of the 20th century.

entries.meaning: Coined by English poet Edmund Spenser to represent Elizabeth I in his poem The Faerie Queene (1590), from Latin glōria (“glory”) + -ana, from Latin -āna, feminine of -ānus (“of or pertaining to”).
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From glory as a variant of the more common Gloria.
entries.note: A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: From Welsh Glyndŵr, from glyn (“valley”) + dŵr (“water”).
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname of Norman origin, name of a 10th-11th-century German saint, from Old High German got (“God”) + harti,herti (“hard, strong”). Brought to England by Normans. Compare Gothard, Godard. * As a French surname, variant of Gaudet.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Old French Godefrei, from Old High German Godafrid (“peace of God”), from Proto-Germanic *Gudafriþuz. Equivalent to god + frith. Doublet of Gottfried and Geoffrey.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From God's way.
entries.note: A male given name used in West Africa, especially Ghana.

entries.meaning: From Old English Godwine (“God's friend”). The component -win is from Old English wine (“friend”). The second meaning is named after Michael Wayne Godwin (born 1956), American attorney and author.
entries.note: A surname originating as a patronymic based on a medieval given name.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname, from the adjective golden. * As an Irish surname, from mag Ualghairg; see McGoldrick.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hebrew גָּלְיָת (golyāṯ).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गोमती (gomatī).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit गोमती (gomatī).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Gongylus, from Ancient Greek Γογγύλος (Gongúlos).
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Spanish Gonzalo.
entries.note: A male given name from Spanish.

entries.meaning: Compound of good + man.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English gōd (“good”) + wine (“friend”).
entries.note: A medieval male given name from Old English, rare today.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Godeve (female given name), from Old English Godġifu (female given name), from god + ġifu. Doublet of Godiva.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname, of rare usage

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Hindi गोपाल (gopāl), etc.
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit गोपाल (gó-pālá).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India, also anglicised as Gopal.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Gordon. Second sense is a pronunciation spelling.

entries.meaning: The main etymology, associated with Celtic names, is from the Scots surname Gordon, from a place name, but the origin is debated: * If the English or Scots name is from a Brythonic language (such as Old Welsh or Old Breton), then possibly from a Proto-Brythonic compound such as *gor (“spacious”) + *din (“fort”); * If the Scots name is itself from English, then possibly from French Gourdon, derived from Gallo-Roman La…

entries.meaning: The commune of France is from Old French Granville, Grandvilla, Grande Villa, Grandivilla, from grant (“grand”) + ville (“settlement”). The surname is of Norman baronial origin, from Grainville, a former commune in Normandy, from the given name Guarin + ville, meaning “Guarin's town”. Guarin ultimately derives from Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: * As an English, Irish, Scottish, and Norman surname, from the placename Graye-sur-Mer in Calvados, from Late Latin Graecus (“Greek”). * Also as an English surname, from the adjective gray. Compare the Irish calque McGreevy. * As a French surname, from Gray, Haute-Saône in France, from the personal name Gradus, a Gallo-Roman/Celtic pronunciation of Gratus, from the name Gratius.
